Even if the reality falls short of the hype, AI will still disrupt the status quo.¶ The United States and China are neck-and-neck in the adoption of AI across their economies and national security ecosystems.
This is not the case with AI. Suspicion, opacity, and uncertainty

on both sides of the Pacific have each state convinced that the other is accelerating AI development in ways that could threaten its security and economic well-being. This perception, rooted in factors that extend far beyond AI itself,
has hardened into a spiral of worst-case assumptions.

One of the most salient concerns is that unforeseen AI breakthroughs might yield unassailable military or economic advantages—the deus ex machina scenario.¶ Over the past decade both states have accelerated the development and adoption of AI. Statements by leaders in Washington about sustaining technological dominance, and by leaders in Beijing about achieving global AI primacy, have shifted the landscape. What was largely a parallel and inward-focused endeavor has become a bilateral competition.

Stability of all kinds¶ Artificial intelligence reshapes both the grammar and the logic of competition, much as nuclear weapons altered great-power relations during the Cold War even when they were only one factor among many. ¶
The concept of strategic stability is central to nuclear deterrence

. In the nuclear era, capabilities were largely observable and, to a significant extent, verifiable. They changed slowly. Intentions were inferred primarily from physical force posture—the positioning and repositioning of aircraft, bombers, and missiles along with observable changes to military alert levels. Stability rested on symmetry and mutual vulnerability. When
both sides believed the other could retaliate decisively, neither had an incentive to strike first

. Indeed the destabilizing characteristics of AI compound one another. First, AI capabilities are difficult to observe and tricky to verify. States cannot see training data, model architectures, integration pathways, or the breadth and depth of adoption. Even access to computing power is observable only indirectly—through energy consumption, supply chain signals, public disclosures, and fragmentary reporting. In such an environment state-level deception becomes easier, cheaper, and more tempting, further obscuring meaningful signals. There is no verification regime capable of producing shared confidence about AI capabilities or intent. These blind spots encourage worst-case planning and competitive escalation.¶ Second,
seamless diffusion from civilian to military

. As with the Kennedy-era Cold War “missile gap” myth—when the United States became convinced that it had fewer intercontinental ballistic missiles than the Soviet Union—threat inflation is a risk when both sides operate near the frontier

. Symmetric capability generates symmetric anxiety rather than stability.¶ Finally, AI is also changing the mental models that each side uses to interpret the other. It alters threat perceptions, expectations about the pace of development, and assumptions about escalation. Information operations enhanced by AI can distort or overwhelm the perceptions of policymakers and military commanders. Even a plausible AI-generated deepfake of a senior leader announcing military action could compress decision timelines before authenticity can be verified. These altered ways of thinking form the foundations for bilateral instability. ¶ Outside of the nuclear ecosystem, a more appropriate concept is bilateral stability. This is how two states in a high-stakes AI competition should navigate perceptions, capabilities, and mechanisms of risk-reduction to minimize the incentives for escalation, misperception, or surprise. Bilateral stability exists within a broader ecosystem of global stability, shaped by the distribution of AI capabilities and norms across allies, partners, competitors, and adversaries.¶
In the AI era, deterrence cannot rest on the promise of permanent technological superiority or
. Neither is durable in a domain defined by rapid diffusion, ambiguity, and continuous adaptation. Instead,
stabilizing objective is not to “win” a notional AI competition. Instead
, it is to deny adversaries confidence that surprise breakthroughs will yield uncontested advantage, while
each side’s belief that escalation remains controllable

. When traditional verification and assurance mechanisms are moot, dialogue, signaling, and the management of uncertainty are crucial to deterrence.¶ Opacity and uncertainty¶ Opacity is baked into contemporary AI competition. Neither the United States nor China can generate sufficient shared situational awareness about how AI is being developed, integrated, or used by the other. In earlier eras of technological competition, institutions such as the U.S. Office of Technology Assessment were able to produce relatively transparent public assessments of emerging innovations and their strategic implications. ¶ AI differs in that its most consequential components are often proprietary, classified, or otherwise inaccessible even to government analysts. This problem stems from many things: hidden model architectures and parameters; undisclosed training data; uncertain access to computing power; privately conducted commercial R&D; classified military applications; unobservable integration pathways; and unverifiable claims about performance. Moreover, to preserve national and military security, the open-source models that have been crucial to global AI innovation will increasingly be complemented—or in some cases deliberately supplanted—by closed-source models designed to limit external scrutiny. ¶ There is also uncertainty surrounding top AI talent within and across national systems. This shapes long-term capability yet is difficult to assess in real time. Plus it is extraordinarily difficult to differentiate between commercial and military uses of AI or defensive and offensive applications, or to anticipate how AI might support new concepts in warfighting. ¶ What is the strategic consequence of these deep information asymmetries? Uncertainty. Neither the United States nor China can draw consistently reliable conclusions about intentions, capabilities, timelines, thresholds for escalation, risk tolerance, and the likelihood of surprise.
Uncertainty drives leaders toward planning for the worst.
It magnifies their perceptions of both vulnerability and opportunity. And it
increases the risk that one side will misread routine development as preparation for
. In such an environment, uncertainty becomes pervasive and self-reinforcing. ¶
A certain level of uncertainty has always been essential

to strategic and operational advantage. Throughout history, states and militaries have relied on denial, deception, and calibrated ‘reveal-conceal’ strategies to keep adversaries off balance and preserve freedom of action.
The challenge with AI is the unprecedented scale of that uncertainty
. In earlier eras, leaders could estimate the outer limits of an adversary’s capabilities. In AI, those limits are far harder to define—and far more likely to shift unexpectedly. ¶

. These asymmetries are intensified by the structural characteristics of AI. The following forms of uncertainty are analytically distinct but operationally inseparable:¶

: uncertainty about the other state’s long-term intentions and strategic goals for AI development. Are they primarily economic, military, prestige-based, or deterrence-centered—and in what proportion? How likely are leaders to take preventive or preemptive action if they believe the other side has achieved a breakthrough?¶

: limited insight into the other side’s schedules for model development, research progress, and timelines to superhuman systems—exacerbated by the absence of a comprehensive, continually-updated comparative assessment of U.S. and Chinese AI capabilities and trajectories.¶

: uncertainty about when and under what conditions political leaders and military commanders will have confidence in AI-enhanced systems and accept, override, or resist their assessments and recommendations.¶ Capability: uncertainty over how much operational advantage AI-enhanced systems may confer across intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance (ISR), targeting, weapon systems, logistics, command and control, and decision support—and for how long.¶

: uncertainty regarding the scale and pace of AI proliferation across military organizations, including how quickly new models, autonomous systems, or agentic tools can be deployed, integrated, used, and updated once in the field.¶ Operations: uncertainty about how AI-enhanced military systems will perform in crisis or conflict, under degraded conditions, in contested cyber environments, and when interacting with other AI systems; or about how such systems will contribute to novel warfighting concepts.¶

: uncertainty about whether and how AI might be incorporated into systems for nuclear command, control, and communications. How could that affect perceptions of, or the extent of, second-strike survivability?¶ Meta: uncertainty about the reliability of the assessments above—how confident leaders should be in their judgments, how much weight to assign them, and how the various factors interact. This second-order uncertainty can magnify instability and heighten the risk of unintended escalation even when individual assessments are directionally correct.¶ In short,
leaders in both capitals face a central dilemma: how many unknowns can they tolerate

? They need to hold on to competitive advantage without tipping into cycles of fear, overreaction, and miscalculation. Put differently, what are they willing to sacrifice to compete in a field defined by rapid and opaque technological change? ¶ Over time,
uncertainty levels can be meaningfully reduced

. Several strategies can help: dedicated intelligence collection, better analytic models, and broader operational experience among military and national security practitioners in using AI-enhanced systems, to name a few. Without these, both sides have few tools beyond official statements, outside analyses, and their own assumptions. In such an environment, the perceived costs of underestimating the other are judged to be far greater than the costs of overestimating and overspending—fueling an escalatory spiral. ¶ Yet opacity and uncertainty alone do not account for the instability of the moment. The narratives through which political and military leaders, analysts, media, and expert communities interpret the AI competition can amplify or distort threat perceptions in ways that mimic material instability. Certain framings make matters worse, especially the language of an ‘AI arms race’ or a ‘race to AGI.’ These encourage policymakers to see AI development as a zero-sum competition. ¶ Manufactured Instability¶ Artificial intelligence is a general-purpose technology. It is a feature of countless systems, not one product. Like electricity or digital networks, it acts as an enabling force across societies and militaries. It comprises a constellation of interconnected capabilities: vast computing power, huge datasets, advanced algorithms, open-source tools, human expertise, and growing energy demands. Unlike weapon systems built exclusively for military use, AI is embedded across the economy. For these reasons,
it makes little sense to speak of an “AI arms race”
any more than of an “electricity arms race.” Characterizing the competition in AI between the United States and China this way manufactures more instability. It
encourages both sides to believe the other is speeding toward AI dominance—a term that is, at best, ill-defined. ¶

The distinction between continuous competition under uncertainty and an arms race is more than semantics. It shapes how states interpret risk, urgency, and restraint. Arms racing implies that capabilities are measurable, progress is observable, and the end state is definable—such as the number of deployed nuclear weapons or delivery platforms. Artificial intelligence fits none of these conditions. Treating AI as a multifaceted, evolving technological competition would not reduce urgency in either capital. But it does not presume a finish line or set of metrics. So it is far less likely to generate destabilizing behavior driven by the illusion that one state might lap or lag the other. ¶ The “first-to-artificial general intelligence (AGI)” narrative introduces similar escalatory pressures. It too assumes a definitive end state. Yet AI development does not proceed in linear or predictable ways, nor will it culminate in a single breakthrough. The focus on AGI in major commercial labs is understandable from a research and commercial standpoint. But for the public sector, the AGI discourse diverts attention from the foundational, long-horizon work required to buy down decades of accumulated technical debt and modernize the nation’s digital infrastructure. ¶ If a U.S. or Chinese company declared tomorrow that it had achieved AGI, the pronouncement would be difficult to verify and would have no immediate relevance for either state’s armed forces. Instead what matters for military effectiveness is how widely and effectively AI is used, how effectively digital modernization is carried out, whether new warfighting concepts evolve around AI-enhanced capabilities, and how military organizations adapt to a digital age. These are the factors that will shape the future balance of military power.¶ Together, misleading narratives can reify worst-case assumptions and narrow the space for rational decision-making. These framings also add fuel to the fire of opacity and uncertainty. Managing these accumulated risks requires deliberate channels of communications designed to reduce misperception, clarify intent, and preserve space for calibrated competition.¶ Bilateral and Multilateral Dialogues¶
should not be judged by their ability to produce diplomatic breakthroughs—be they official (Track I), semi-official (Track 1.5), or unofficial (Track II). They should instead be understood as

. The 2024 agreement by Presidents Biden and Xi to maintain human control over nuclear-weapon use, for example, was enabled by years of quiet deliberations, across Track II, Track 1.5, and Track I channels.¶ These dialogues are instrumental, not aspirational. They are grounded in the recognition that many AI-related challenges to stability and security are shared. Their purpose is to
help stabilize relations while acknowledging the primacy of national self-interests. Dialogue

—if not always agreement—on definitions and key terms. It can: identify catastrophic and existential risks; manage perceptions; explore national and global approaches to AI governance, risk management, and model practices; discuss AI redlines; propose confidence-building measures; and explore mechanisms for verification. Discussions about realistic scenarios can highlight risks and identify potential mitigation strategies. ¶ Artificial intelligence is still novel enough, and spans such a wide range of military and civilian applications, that it merits dedicated dialogues—at least at the Track II and Track 1.5 levels. At the Track I level, AI could be incorporated into broader discussions on technology, security, or crisis management. With sustained Track 1 meetings looking unlikely in the near term, Track II and Track 1.5 channels take on added importance. They allow communication to continue, provide informal two-way feedback between official and unofficial communities, and shape the conditions for restarting Track 1 discussions when political circumstances permit. This approach requires alignment and consistency across all tracks. Mixed messages or, worse, statements that conflict with official positions, can undermine credibility, reduce effectiveness, and erode the trust needed to reduce risk. ¶ These
forms of engagement cannot eliminate uncertainty. They can help make it more manageable

, even while each side acknowledges that some uncertainty is essential to each country’s economy and security. Prior Track II dialogues have produced concrete outputs, in addition to the Biden-Xi agreement on AI and nuclear weapons. These include: AI glossaries; a draft AI Code of Conduct; model practices for AI test and evaluation; a framework for risk management in AI-enabled military systems; and recommendations on mitigating the risks at the intersection of AI and biotechnology. Future dialogues will continue to explore other potential confidence-building mechanisms.
